fixed.q: Which program acts as a bridge (intermediary) between the computer user and the computer hardware?
fixed.w: The OS is the intermediary between user and hardware, and also the resource manager and the platform for applications.

fixed.q: The primary goal of an operating system is:
fixed.w: Primary goal = convenience. Efficiency, reliability and maintainability are secondary goals.

fixed.q: Which of these services is NOT provided by the operating system?
o: Translating source code into machine code
fixed.w: Translation is the compiler's job, not an OS service.

fixed.q: Which is the desirable property of a good operating system?
o: High throughput and low turnaround time
Low throughput and low turnaround time
High throughput and high turnaround time
Low throughput and high turnaround time
fixed.w: Maximise throughput (jobs finished per unit time); minimise turnaround time.

fixed.q: In a multiprogramming system, what happens when the running job has to wait for I/O?
o: The OS switches the CPU to another job in memory
The CPU sits idle until the I/O completes
The job is swapped to tape
fixed.w: Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory so the CPU is never idle while at least one job can run.

fixed.q: Multiprogramming was made possible by:
o: I/O units that work independently of the CPU, together with OS support
Only the operating system, without any hardware support
fixed.w: Independent I/O units (channels, DMA) let the CPU run another job during I/O, and the OS schedules them. The key's answer is 'both'.

fixed.q: Time-sharing (multitasking) is best described as:
o: Multiprogramming with frequent switching (round robin) so each user feels the computer is dedicated to them
Several CPUs running processes in true parallel
fixed.w: Time-sharing = multiprogramming + time slices; context switching gives the illusion of parallelism.

fixed.q: Which is NOT an advantage of a multiprocessing system?
fixed.w: Coordinating several CPUs increases OS overhead and complexity.

fixed.q: Car airbag controllers need a deadline that must never be missed. They use a:
fixed.w: Hard real-time: a late result is useless. Soft real-time (multimedia, phones) tolerates occasional misses.

fixed.q: Match: (a) Multiprocessing (b) Multithreading (c) Multiuser with (i) many users share devices such as printers at once (ii) two or more CPUs shared by programs (iii) a program broken into smaller parts loaded as needed.
fixed.w: Multiprocessing = several CPUs; multithreading = program split into parts (threads); multiuser = users sharing devices.

fixed.q: An operating system that lets computers share files across a network is a:
fixed.w: A network OS provides file and printer sharing across a network.

fixed.q: Which of the following is NOT an operating system for mobile devices?
fixed.w: MANET is a type of ad-hoc network, not an OS.

fixed.q: Spooling (as in a printer queue) means:
o: Holding data temporarily in memory or disk until a slow device is ready for it
Sharing the CPU in time slices
fixed.w: SPOOL = Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line; e.g. print jobs wait in a queue on disk.

fixed.q: Which statement about kernels is FALSE?
o: In a monolithic kernel, user services and kernel services are kept in separate address spaces
A microkernel is smaller in size
A monolithic kernel is not easy to extend
Microkernel designs keep the file system and device drivers in user space
fixed.w: A monolithic kernel keeps both in the SAME address space; separating them is what a microkernel does.

fixed.q: In the microkernel approach, which services stay inside the kernel?
o: IPC, basic memory management and CPU scheduling
fixed.w: Mach-style microkernel keeps only IPC, memory management and scheduling; file system and drivers run in user mode, using message passing.

fixed.q: Which of these is a monolithic-kernel OS (as per the exam key)?
fixed.w: Linux is monolithic. Mach and MINIX 3 are microkernels (MINIX 3 by Tanenbaum, ~12,000 lines). The DSSSB key also treats Windows as monolithic.

fixed.q: In the layered approach, layer 0 is the:
fixed.w: Layer 0 = hardware; the top layer (N) = user interface.

fixed.q: The memory-resident components of an operating system are commonly called the:
fixed.w: The kernel is the core that stays in memory.

fixed.q: Which of the following is NOT a Linux/UNIX shell?
fixed.w: Shells: Bourne (sh), C shell (csh), Korn (ksh), Bourne-Again (bash).

fixed.q: To access the services of the operating system, the interface is provided by:
fixed.w: System calls are the interface to OS services; programmers usually reach them through an API (e.g. printf() calls write()).

fixed.q: The 'wait for time' system call belongs to which category?
fixed.w: Process control: end/abort, load/execute, create/terminate, get/set attributes, wait for time, wait/signal event, allocate/free memory.

fixed.q: Which operation belongs to the communications category of system calls?
o: Create or delete a communication connection
fixed.w: Communications: create/delete connection, send/receive messages, transfer status, attach/detach remote devices.

fixed.q: Which of the following is NOT a system-call category?
fixed.w: The six categories: process control, file management, device management, information maintenance, communications, protection.

fixed.q: The hardware mode bit for kernel mode and user mode is:
o: It depends on the process priority
fixed.w: Mode bit 0 = kernel (privileged), 1 = user. A system call traps into kernel mode and the bit returns to 1 afterwards.

fixed.q: At the end of kernel bootstrap in UNIX, which process is started?
fixed.w: After bootstrap the kernel starts init (PID 1). The scheduler/swapper is PID 0.

fixed.q: In UNIX, the PID of the kernel's scheduler (swapper) process is:
fixed.w: Swapper/scheduler = PID 0; init = PID 1.

fixed.q: Which is loaded into main memory when the computer is booted?
o: Internal command instructions (the resident part of the OS)
fixed.w: In DOS, COMMAND.COM with internal commands (DIR, COPY) is loaded; external commands stay on disk.

fixed.q: A program becomes a process when:
o: It is loaded into main memory and its PCB is created
It is opened in an editor
fixed.w: A program is a passive file on disk; a process is an active entity with a PCB in memory.

fixed.q: Which section of a process in memory holds local variables, function parameters and return addresses?
fixed.w: Text = code; Data = globals; Heap = dynamic allocation; Stack = locals, parameters, return addresses.

fixed.q: Which of these is NOT stored in the Process Control Block?
o: The source code of the program
fixed.w: PCB: state, PC, registers, scheduling info, memory-management info, accounting info, I/O status (open files).

fixed.q: Match the states: I. New  II. Running  III. Ready with 1. waiting to be assigned a processor  2. instructions being executed  3. being created.
fixed.w: New = being created; Running = executing; Ready = waiting for the CPU.

fixed.q: Which of the following is NOT a process state?
fixed.w: States: new, ready, running, waiting (blocked), terminated.

fixed.q: A running process moves to the ready state when:
o: An interrupt occurs (e.g. its time quantum expires)
fixed.w: Running→Ready = interrupt/pre-emption; Running→Waiting = I/O or event wait; Waiting→Ready = I/O completion; Running→Terminated = exit.

fixed.q: The OS completely releases the memory allocated to a process after it moves:
fixed.w: Memory is fully freed only when the process terminates.

fixed.q: Which scheduler controls the degree of multiprogramming by admitting jobs from the job pool?
fixed.w: LTS admits jobs and should pick a good mix of CPU-bound and I/O-bound processes. It runs least often.

fixed.q: Swapping processes out of memory and back in is done by the:
fixed.w: The medium-term scheduler suspends/swaps processes to reduce the degree of multiprogramming.

fixed.q: Lifting a process from memory and placing it on disk is called:
fixed.w: Memory → disk = swap out; disk → memory = swap in. Removing suspended processes and later returning them = swapping.

fixed.q: Which part of the OS gives the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler?
fixed.w: Dispatcher: context switch, switch to user mode, jump to the right place in the program. Its delay = dispatch latency.

fixed.q: I. On a context switch the kernel saves the old process's context in its PCB. II. Context-switch time is pure overhead. Which is correct?
fixed.w: Both true: state is saved to the PCB, and no useful work is done during the switch.

fixed.q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Burst time is the time a process takes to start its execution
Turnaround time = completion time − arrival time
Completion time is when the process finishes
Arrival time is when the process enters the ready queue
fixed.w: Burst time is the CPU time the process NEEDS. TAT = CT − AT; WT = TAT − BT.

fixed.q: Waiting time in CPU scheduling is the total time a process spends:
fixed.w: Scheduling only changes the time spent waiting in the ready queue, not the burst or I/O time.

fixed.q: Which of the following is NOT a CPU scheduling algorithm?
fixed.w: C-SCAN is a disk-scheduling algorithm. SJN = shortest job next = SJF.

fixed.q: The convoy effect is a drawback of:
fixed.w: In FCFS, short processes wait behind a long one, raising average waiting time.

fixed.q: Which algorithm gives the minimum average waiting time and is used as the benchmark?
fixed.w: SJF/SRTF is optimal for average waiting time but can't be implemented exactly (next burst must be predicted).

fixed.q: I. SRTF may cause starvation. II. Round Robin is better than FCFS in response time. Which is true?
fixed.w: Long jobs may starve under SRTF; RR gives the best response time.

fixed.q: The standard solution to starvation in priority scheduling is:
o: Ageing: gradually raising the priority of waiting processes
Lowering the priority of new processes
fixed.w: Ageing prevents indefinite blocking.

fixed.q: In Round Robin, if the time quantum is made very large, RR behaves like:
fixed.w: Large q → fewer switches, worse response, effectively FCFS. Very small q → many context switches, lower CPU utilisation.

fixed.q: With n processes in the ready queue and time quantum q, the maximum time a process waits for its next turn in RR is:
fixed.w: Each of the other n − 1 processes can use at most one quantum before it runs again.

fixed.q: In multilevel FEEDBACK queue scheduling, unlike plain multilevel queue scheduling:
o: Processes can move between queues based on their CPU-burst behaviour
Processes are permanently assigned to one queue
fixed.w: MLFQ demotes CPU-heavy processes and promotes long-waiting ones (ageing). It is the most general and most complex algorithm.

fixed.q: A thread is also known as a:
fixed.w: A thread is the basic unit of CPU utilisation: own thread ID, PC, registers and stack; shares code, data and open files with its process.

fixed.q: Which of these is NOT shared among threads of the same process?
fixed.w: Each thread has its own stack, registers and program counter.

fixed.q: I. Threads encapsulate concurrency within a process. II. A process encapsulates protection within the system. Which is true?
fixed.w: Thread = unit of concurrency; process = unit of protection/resource ownership.

fixed.q: I. Threads in a process are visible to other processes. II. A thread is strictly a private resource of its process. Which is true?
fixed.w: Threads are private to their process and are not visible to other processes.

fixed.q: In the many-to-one threading model:
o: A blocking system call blocks the whole process
Each user thread maps to its own kernel thread
The process can use several CPUs in parallel
There is no limit on threads and nothing blocks
fixed.w: Many-to-one: one kernel thread, so one block blocks all and no multi-CPU use. One-to-one (Linux, Windows) fixes this at more overhead; many-to-many gives the best of both.

fixed.q: fork() and ___ are used together to make a complete process subroutine (create and merge concurrent paths).
fixed.w: fork creates a concurrent path, join merges it back.

fixed.q: The return value of fork() in the child process is:
fixed.w: Child gets 0; parent gets the child's PID (positive); −1 on failure.

fixed.q: The endpoint of inter-process (network) communication is a:
fixed.w: A socket = IP address + port, the endpoint of communication.

fixed.q: A process that can affect or be affected by other processes executing in the system is a:
fixed.w: Cooperating processes share data; independent processes don't.

fixed.q: A situation where two or more processes access shared data concurrently and the result depends on the order of execution is a:
fixed.w: Race condition: output depends on the interleaving.

fixed.q: Which critical-section requirement guarantees that no process waits forever (no starvation)?
fixed.w: Bounded waiting limits how many times others can enter before a waiting process gets in. Many Indian notes call ME and progress mandatory and bounded waiting desirable; Galvin requires all three.

fixed.q: The two-process solution using only a shared 'turn' variable fails which requirement?
fixed.w: 'turn' gives ME but strict alternation, so progress fails. The 'flag' array solution can deadlock. Peterson and Dekker satisfy all three.

fixed.q: Peterson's solution satisfies:
o: Mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting, for two processes
Only mutual exclusion, for n processes
Mutual exclusion and progress, but not bounded waiting
fixed.w: Peterson uses both flag[] and turn; it is a correct 2-process software solution.

fixed.q: A semaphore is an integer variable that, apart from initialisation, is accessed only through which atomic operations?
fixed.w: wait = P (proberen), signal = V (verhogen).

fixed.q: Which of the following is a synchronisation tool?
fixed.w: Pipes and sockets are communication tools; semaphores synchronise.

fixed.q: Process synchronisation can be done at:
fixed.w: Software: Peterson, semaphores. Hardware: test-and-set, disabling interrupts.

fixed.q: A semaphore whose wait() loops 'while (S <= 0);' is called a spinlock. Its main drawback is:
o: It works only for two processes
fixed.w: The waiting process keeps testing S instead of blocking. Semaphores work for n processes; implementations with a waiting queue avoid busy waiting.

fixed.q: In the producer–consumer problem with an n-slot buffer, the semaphores are initialised as:
fixed.w: empty counts empty slots (starts n), full counts filled slots (starts 0), mutex guards the buffer.

fixed.q: In the readers–writers solution, the first reader does wait(wrt) and the last reader does signal(wrt). This allows:
o: Many readers at once, but a writer only alone
Only one reader at a time
fixed.w: Readers share; a writer needs exclusive access.

fixed.q: In the naive dining-philosophers solution (each picks left then right chopstick), the problem is:
o: It can deadlock if all pick up their left chopstick at once
It violates mutual exclusion on chopsticks
It needs a binary semaphore per philosopher
fixed.w: Fixes: at most 4 at the table, pick both only if both free, or odd/even pick in opposite order.

fixed.q: A set of processes is deadlocked when:
o: Each process is waiting for an event that only another process in the set can cause
One process uses too much CPU
fixed.w: Permanent blocking on events that will never occur.

fixed.q: Which deadlock condition says at least one resource must be held in a non-sharable mode?
fixed.w: All four (ME, hold and wait, no pre-emption, circular wait) must hold at the same time.

fixed.q: Numbering all resource types and letting processes request them only in increasing order prevents deadlock by removing:
fixed.w: Ordering breaks the cycle. Requesting all resources up front removes hold and wait.

fixed.q: Which deadlock condition can generally NOT be removed for prevention?
fixed.w: Some resources (printers) are intrinsically non-sharable.

fixed.q: The Banker's algorithm is a deadlock ___ technique.
fixed.w: It needs each process's maximum demand in advance and grants a request only if the state stays safe. Need = Max − Allocation.

fixed.q: Which statement about safe and unsafe states is correct?
o: An unsafe state may lead to deadlock but is not necessarily a deadlock
An unsafe state is always a deadlock
A safe state may contain a deadlock
Safe states have no safe sequence
fixed.w: Deadlock ⊂ unsafe. Safe = at least one safe sequence exists.

fixed.q: In a resource-allocation graph where every resource has only ONE instance, a cycle is:
fixed.w: With multiple instances a cycle is only necessary.

fixed.q: On recovery from deadlock by termination, the processes to abort are those whose termination incurs:
fixed.w: Select the victim with the least cost.

fixed.q: During resource pre-emption, the solution to starvation of the same victim is:
o: Including the number of rollbacks in the cost factor
Including the number of resources in pre-emption
fixed.w: Otherwise the same process may always be picked as victim.

fixed.q: Ignoring deadlocks and restarting when one happens is called the:
fixed.w: Used by many OSs because deadlocks are rare and detection is costly.

fixed.q: Which address is generated by the CPU?
fixed.w: The CPU generates logical (virtual) addresses; the MMU translates them to physical addresses.

fixed.q: A partition of 80K given to a 60K process wastes 20K that no other process can use. This is:
fixed.w: Waste inside an allocated partition = internal. Free total enough but not contiguous = external.

fixed.q: Free holes of size a and b exist with a + b > c, but a < c and b < c, so a process of size c can't be placed. This is:
fixed.w: Fixes: compaction, or non-contiguous allocation (paging).

fixed.q: Which placement policy searches the whole free list and picks the SMALLEST hole that is big enough?
fixed.w: Worst fit picks the largest hole; first fit the first big-enough hole; next fit continues from the last allocation. Standard notes: best fit suits fixed partitions, worst fit variable partitions.

fixed.q: With paging there is no ___ fragmentation.
fixed.w: Paging can still have internal fragmentation in the last page.

fixed.q: Which is used as an index into the page table?
fixed.w: Logical address = (page number p, offset d); p indexes the page table, which gives the frame number.

fixed.q: The address of the page table in memory is held by the:
fixed.w: PTBR points to the start of the current process's page table.

fixed.q: Which table contains the base address of each page in physical memory?
fixed.w: Each page-table entry gives the frame (base address) for that page.

fixed.q: Which statement about page tables is correct?
o: Each process has its own page table, stored in main memory
There is one page table in hardware for all processes
The page table is stored in the CPU registers
The page table has one entry per physical frame
fixed.w: One entry per frame is the INVERTED page table, which has only one table in the system.

fixed.q: Making the page size larger results in:
o: More internal fragmentation and a smaller page table
Less internal fragmentation and a smaller page table
More internal fragmentation and a larger page table
Less internal fragmentation and a larger page table
fixed.w: Bigger pages → fewer pages (smaller table) but more waste in the last page.

fixed.q: The TLB is a:
o: Small, fast associative memory caching page-table entries
Part of the disk used for swapping
fixed.w: TLB hit avoids the extra memory access. It must be flushed on context switches unless entries are wired down.

fixed.q: In segmentation, a logical address consists of:
o: Segment number and offset, checked against the segment's limit
fixed.w: Segment table entry = (base, limit). Offset ≥ limit → trap. Segments are variable sized, so segmentation suffers external fragmentation.

fixed.q: Which technique gives the illusion of a main memory much larger than the physical RAM, using disk space?
fixed.w: Asked many times: secondary memory addressed as though it were main memory.

fixed.q: A page fault occurs when:
o: The referenced page is not in main memory
The page is corrupted by software
The page is in main memory
fixed.w: Page fault = valid-invalid bit is invalid; the OS traps and loads the page.

fixed.q: The rate at which page faults occur is known as the:
fixed.w: EAT = (1 − p) × ma + p × page-fault service time, p = page-fault rate.

fixed.q: ___ contains the swap space.
fixed.w: Swap space is an area on the disk.

fixed.q: A scheme where only a portion of a job's address space is actually loaded into physical memory is:
fixed.w: Pure demand paging starts with zero pages and loads a page only on a fault.

fixed.q: Increasing the RAM of a computer typically improves performance because:
fixed.w: More frames → fewer page faults.

fixed.q: The modify (dirty) bit of a page is used to:
o: Avoid writing an unmodified victim page back to disk
fixed.w: If the dirty bit is not set, the disk copy is already correct, so only the swap-in is needed.

fixed.q: Which page-replacement algorithm suffers from Belady's anomaly?
fixed.w: Belady: more frames → more faults, for FIFO. LRU and OPT are stack algorithms and never show it.

fixed.q: Which page-replacement algorithm gives the lowest page-fault rate but cannot be implemented?
o: Optimal (replace the page not used for the longest time in future)
fixed.w: OPT needs future knowledge, so it's used as a benchmark.

fixed.q: A process is thrashing if:
o: It spends more time paging than executing
It spends more time executing than paging
No memory has been allocated to it
fixed.w: High paging activity, CPU utilisation collapses as multiprogramming increases.

fixed.q: If the working-set window Δ is too large, it:
o: Will not encompass the entire locality
fixed.w: Too small → misses the locality; too large → overlaps several localities.

fixed.q: Which statement about localities is true?
o: A program is generally composed of several different localities, which may overlap
A program has exactly one locality
fixed.w: From the locality model: several localities that may overlap.

fixed.q: The time a disk takes to position the head on the selected track is the:
fixed.w: Total time = seek + rotational latency (avg half a rotation) + transfer.

fixed.q: The advantage of SSTF disk scheduling is:
o: Overhead of calculating seek time in advance
fixed.w: SSTF lowers average seek and response time, but can starve far requests.

fixed.q: Which disk-scheduling algorithm jumps back to the start without serving requests on the return trip?
fixed.w: SCAN reverses and serves on the way back (elevator). C-SCAN gives more uniform waiting. LOOK/C-LOOK go only as far as the last request.

fixed.q: Which statement is true?
o: A block device transfers a block of bytes as a unit
A block device transfers one byte at a time
A block device always has unpredictable response times
A keyboard is a block device
fixed.w: Disks = block devices; keyboards = character devices.

fixed.q: An asynchronous (non-blocking) I/O call:
o: Returns immediately without waiting for the I/O to complete
fixed.w: Completion is signalled later.

fixed.q: Which file-allocation method supports only sequential access?
fixed.w: Contiguous: sequential + direct, but external fragmentation. Indexed: direct access, index-block overhead.

fixed.q: A UNIX inode has 15 block pointers. How many of them point directly to data blocks?
fixed.w: 12 direct + 1 single indirect + 1 double indirect + 1 triple indirect.

fixed.q: In a free-space bit vector, a bit value of 1 usually means the block is:
fixed.w: Bit map: 1 = free, 0 = allocated (as in the standard textbook).

fixed.q: The 'volume control block' (UNIX superblock) in a file system contains:
o: Volume details such as the number of blocks, block size and free-block count
The unique identifier linking a file to its directory entry
fixed.w: Per-file details are in the FCB/inode; the boot control block holds boot information.

fixed.q: Which file operation need not involve any actual I/O and is also called a 'file seek'?
fixed.w: Only the current-position pointer changes.

fixed.q: A: Creating a file requires space to be allocated in the file system. B: An entry for the new file must be made in the directory. Which is true?
fixed.w: Both steps are needed to create a file.

fixed.q: Making each file's contents contiguous and creating larger free areas is ___; making files take less space is ___.
Which statement about NTFS is NOT true?
o: It does not support compression of files and folders
It uses disk space efficiently with smaller clusters
It has attributes like read-only, hidden, archive, compressed
fixed.w: NTFS DOES support file and folder compression.

fixed.q: The protection domain of a process contains:
fixed.w: A domain is a set of (object, rights-set) pairs.

fixed.q: The global-table implementation of the access matrix stores ordered triples of:
fixed.w: <domain, object, rights-set>. ACL = a column (per object); capability list = a row (per domain).

fixed.q: An access-control list (ACL) corresponds to which part of the access matrix?
fixed.w: Capability list = a row (per subject/domain).

fixed.q: Which component keeps state information about the use of I/O components (open-file tables, device status)?
fixed.w: The kernel I/O subsystem keeps these state tables. (The SSC key option was 'Kernel'.)

fixed.q: Windows NT implements I/O using:
fixed.w: I/O request packets travel between drivers.

fixed.q: The information about a file needed by the system programs that access its records is in:
o: The file header and the file descriptor
fixed.w: Both the file header and the file descriptor hold it (key answer: both).

fixed.q: Test-and-Set is an example of which kind of critical-section solution?
fixed.w: Hardware solutions: atomic test-and-set / swap instructions, or disabling interrupts on a single CPU. Busy waiting is used: while(test_and_set(&lock));

fixed.q: An inverted page table has:
o: One entry per physical frame and only one table in the whole system
One entry per page for each process
Two levels of tables per process
fixed.w: Each entry stores (pid, virtual page). It saves memory but is slower to search.

fixed.q: In symmetric multiprocessing (SMP):
o: All processors are equal and any processor can run any task
Each processor has a fixed, dedicated role
Only one processor runs the OS and others run user jobs
fixed.w: Asymmetric multiprocessing gives each processor a specific role (e.g. a master runs the OS). Multiprocessing systems are tightly coupled; distributed systems are loosely coupled.

fixed.q: Which file access method is best suited to databases?
fixed.w: Direct access treats a file as numbered blocks readable in any order. Editors and compilers use sequential access.

fixed.q: Which of the following page replacement algorithms(s) does not suffer from Belady's anomaly in Operating System? I. Least-Recently Used (LRU) page replacement. II. First-In, First-Out (FIFO) page replacement.
fixed.w: LRU is a stack algorithm and does not suffer from Belady's anomaly; FIFO does.

fixed.q: Page fault means:
o: accessing the page that is not currently in the memory
removing the page whenever it is needed
fetching the page whenever it is needed
an error that always occurs in the page
fixed.w: A page fault occurs when the referenced page is not in main memory.

fixed.q: Which of the following is a storage allocation scheme in which secondary memory can be addressed as though it were part of the main memory?
fixed.w: Virtual memory lets secondary storage be addressed as if it were main memory.

fixed.q: If a memory partition of size 80k is allocated to a process of size 60k then the 20k of the partition is wasted and cannot be allocated to any process. It is called ______.
fixed.w: Unused space inside an allocated partition is internal fragmentation.

fixed.q: Consider a main memory with the capacity of 4 page frames which are initially empty. If the page reference string is 1, 3, 4, 4, 3, 2, 1, 7, 5, 6 then what is the number of page fault using FIFO page replacement algorithm?
fixed.w: FIFO with 4 frames: faults on 1, 3, 4, 2 (4 faults); 1 hits; 7, 5 and 6 each fault. Total 7.

fixed.q: The technique of using disk space to give a program the impression of more random access memory (RAM) than is actually available in the system is called
fixed.w: Virtual memory uses disk (swap or page file) to extend the apparent size of main memory.

fixed.q: Which of the following statements is true?
o: A process is thrashing if it spends a lot of time executing instead of paging.
A process is thrashing if it spends a lot of time paging instead of executing.
A process is thrashing if no memory has been allocated to it.
fixed.w: Thrashing means the process spends more time servicing page faults than doing useful work.

fixed.q: Which of the following statements is true?
o: A program is generally composed of several different localities, which may overlap.
A program is generally composed of several different localities, which must overlap.
A program is generally composed of several different localities, which do not overlap.
A program is generally composed of several different localities, which must not overlap.
fixed.w: This is the locality model (Galvin): a program moves between localities, and localities may overlap.

fixed.q: Consider the page reference string 1 2 3 4 2 1 5 6 2 1 2 3 7 6 3 2 1 2 3 6. For the FIFO page replacement algorithm with 4 frames (the first 4 unique pages also count as page faults), the number of page faults is
fixed.w: Working through FIFO with 4 frames gives faults at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 2, 1, 3, 7, 6, 2, 1, 3 = 14 faults.

fixed.q: A process refers to 5 pages A, B, C, D and E in the order A, B, C, D, A, B, E, A, B, C, D, E. If the page replacement algorithm is FIFO, how many page transfers occur with an empty internal store of 4 frames?
fixed.w: With 4 frames FIFO gives 10 faults (A B C D, then E, A, B, C, D, E). With 3 frames it gives 9: this is Belady's anomaly.

fixed.q: If a processor has a 32-bit virtual address, a 28-bit physical address and 2 KB pages, how many bits are required for the virtual and physical page number?
fixed.w: 2 KB pages need an 11-bit offset. Virtual page number = 32 − 11 = 21 bits. Physical frame number = 28 − 11 = 17 bits.

fixed.q:
The address sequence generated by tracing a particular program executing in a pure demand paging system with 100 records per page, with 1 free main memory frame, is recorded as follows. What is the number of page faults?
0100, 0200, 0430, 0499, 0510, 0530, 0560, 0120, 0220, 0240, 0260, 0320, 0370
fixed.w: The page numbers are 1, 2, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3. With one frame, a fault happens on every change: 1, 2, 4, 5, 1, 2, 3 = 7 faults (GATE 1994 style). The pair options are odd, but only C starts with 7.

List filenames beginning with the pattern 'doc'

bin: It contains executable files for the UNIX commands.

cut the columns/fields of a specified file

Turn Around Time: Time difference between the completion time and arrival time
Completion Time: Time at which a process completes its execution
Arrival Time: Time at which a process arrives in the ready queue

theory.OS basics:
• OS = intermediary between user and hardware, resource manager/allocator, platform for applications.
• Primary goal: convenience. Secondary: efficiency, reliability, maintainability.
• Functions: process, memory, I/O device, file, network management; security & protection.
• Good OS: high throughput, low turnaround time.
• Not an OS service: translating source code (that is the compiler).
theory.Types of OS:
• Batch: similar jobs grouped; CPU idle during slow I/O.
• Multiprogramming: many jobs in memory; CPU switches when a job waits for I/O. Made possible by independent I/O units (DMA/channels) + OS.
• Time-sharing/multitasking: multiprogramming + round-robin time slices → illusion of parallelism.
• Multiprocessing (tightly coupled): many CPUs, true parallelism; SMP = all CPUs equal, AMP = fixed roles. Raises OS overhead.
• Distributed (loosely coupled): networked nodes; resource sharing, speed-up, reliability, communication.
• Real-time: hard (deadline never missed, e.g. airbags) vs soft (occasional miss OK, multimedia).
• Network OS shares files over a network. Mobile OS: Symbian, Palm, Windows Mobile, Android, iOS (MANET is a network type, not an OS).
• SPOOL = Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line (print queue).
theory.OS structure:
• Simple (MS-DOS): not modular.
• Layered: layer 0 = hardware, layer N = user interface.
• Monolithic (Linux): user and kernel services in the SAME address space; hard to extend.
• Microkernel (Mach, CMU; MINIX 3 ~12,000 lines, Tanenbaum): kernel keeps only IPC, memory management, CPU scheduling; file system & drivers run in user space via message passing. Small, easy to extend.
• Kernel = memory-resident core of the OS.
• Shells: Bourne (sh), C shell, Korn, Bash. CLI vs GUI.
theory.System calls:
• System call = interface to OS services; usually reached through an API (printf() → write()).
• Six categories: process control (end/abort, load/execute, create/terminate, wait for time, wait/signal event, allocate/free memory), file management, device management, information maintenance, communications (create/delete connection, send/receive messages, attach/detach remote devices), protection.
• 'Data compilation' is NOT a category.
• Mode bit: kernel = 0, user = 1. A system call traps into kernel mode.
theory.Booting:
• Boot loads the resident part of the OS (DOS: COMMAND.COM with internal commands DIR, COPY; external commands stay on disk).
• UNIX: scheduler/swapper = PID 0; init = PID 1, started at the end of kernel bootstrap (/etc/init).
theory.Process:
• Process = program in execution (active). Program = passive file on disk; becomes a process when loaded into memory and its PCB is created.
• Memory sections: text (code), data (globals), heap (dynamic), stack (locals, parameters, return addresses).
• PCB: state, program counter, CPU registers, scheduling info, memory-management info, accounting info, I/O status (open files).
• States: new, ready, running, waiting (blocked), terminated.
• Transitions: new→ready admitted; ready→running dispatch; running→ready interrupt/quantum expiry; running→waiting I/O wait; waiting→ready I/O done; running→terminated exit. Memory fully freed only on termination.
theory.Schedulers:
• Long-term (job) scheduler: admits jobs, controls degree of multiprogramming, picks CPU-/I/O-bound mix; runs least often.
• Short-term (CPU) scheduler: picks the next ready process; runs most often.
• Medium-term: swaps processes out/in (memory→disk = swap out).
• Dispatcher gives the CPU to the chosen process: context switch, switch to user mode, jump to the right instruction. Its delay = dispatch latency.
theory.Context switch:
• Save old process state into its PCB, load new process state from its PCB.
• Context-switch time is pure overhead (no useful work).
theory.CPU scheduling:
• AT arrival, BT burst (CPU time needed), CT completion. TAT = CT − AT. WT = TAT − BT. Response time = first run − AT.
• Maximise CPU utilisation and throughput; minimise TAT, WT, response time.
• FCFS: non-pre-emptive, FIFO queue, convoy effect.
• SJF (non-pre-emptive) / SRTF (pre-emptive): minimum average WT (optimal benchmark); can starve long jobs; next burst must be predicted.
• Priority: can starve low priority → fix with ageing.
• Round Robin: time quantum q; best response time; max wait (n−1)q; huge q → FCFS, tiny q → too many context switches.
• Multilevel queue: processes fixed to a queue. Multilevel feedback queue: processes move between queues; most general and most complex.
• Gantt-chart method: at each decision point pick by the algorithm's rule; ties → arrival order. C-SCAN is disk, not CPU, scheduling.
theory.Threads:
• Thread = lightweight process: own thread ID, PC, registers, stack; shares code, data, open files with its process.
• Thread = unit of concurrency; process = unit of protection/resource ownership. Threads are private to their process.
• Models: many-to-one (one block blocks all, no multi-CPU), one-to-one (Linux, Windows; more overhead, thread limit), many-to-many (best of both, complex).
theory.fork:
• fork() copies the calling process. Returns 0 in the child, the child's PID (positive) in the parent, −1 on failure.
• n fork() calls in sequence → 2ⁿ processes in total, 2ⁿ − 1 new children; a printf after them runs 2ⁿ times.
• fork and join together create and merge concurrent paths.
theory.IPC:
• Cooperating processes can affect or be affected by others (share data); independent ones can't.
• IPC by shared memory or message passing. Socket = endpoint of communication (IP + port). Pipes and sockets are communication tools; semaphores are synchronisation tools.
theory.Synchronisation:
• Race condition: result depends on the order of execution on shared data.
• Critical-section requirements: mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting (in Indian notes ME + progress are 'mandatory', bounded waiting 'desirable'; failing it → starvation).
• turn variable: ME yes, progress no (strict alternation). flag array: can deadlock. Peterson & Dekker: all three (2 processes).
• Semaphore: integer accessed only via atomic wait (P) and signal (V). Counting vs binary (mutex). Busy-waiting version = spinlock.
• Producer–consumer: mutex = 1, empty = n, full = 0.
• Readers–writers: first reader waits on wrt, last reader signals it; many readers or one writer.
• Dining philosophers: naive left-then-right can deadlock; fixes: max 4 seated, pick both together, odd/even order.
• Hardware: test-and-set, disabling interrupts. Synchronisation can be done in hardware and software.
theory.Deadlock:
• Deadlock: every process in a set waits for an event only another process in the set can cause.
• Four necessary conditions together: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption, circular wait.
• Handling: prevention (break a condition: ordering resources breaks circular wait; requesting all at once breaks hold-and-wait; mutual exclusion usually can't be broken), avoidance (Banker's, needs max demand), detection + recovery, ignorance (ostrich).
• Safe state = a safe sequence exists; unsafe may lead to deadlock (deadlock ⊂ unsafe).
• RAG: cycle necessary; with single-instance resources a cycle is necessary and sufficient.
• Recovery: abort all, or one at a time choosing minimum cost; pre-emption with rollback; include rollback count in cost to avoid starving the same victim.
theory.Banker's algorithm:
• Need = Max − Allocation. Available = Total − Σ Allocation.
• Safety check: Work = Available. Repeatedly find a process with Need ≤ Work, run it, then Work += its Allocation. If all finish → safe, and the order is a safe sequence.
• If at some point no remaining process fits → unsafe.
• Complexity about m × n².
theory.Memory:
• CPU generates logical addresses; the MMU (relocation + limit registers) maps them to physical addresses; out-of-limit → trap.
• Contiguous allocation: first fit (first big enough), best fit (smallest big enough), worst fit (largest), next fit (continue from last).
• Internal fragmentation: waste inside an allocated block (fixed partitions, paging). External: enough total free space but not contiguous (variable partitions, segmentation). Fix external by compaction or non-contiguous allocation.
theory.Memory allocation:
• First fit: scan from the start, take the first hole ≥ request.
• Best fit: smallest hole ≥ request. Worst fit: largest hole.
• After placing, the hole shrinks by the process size; a process that fits nowhere must wait.
• Classic: holes 100, 500, 200, 300, 600 with 212, 417, 112, 426 → only best fit places all.
theory.Paging:
• Process split into pages, memory into frames of the same size. No external fragmentation; small internal fragmentation in the last page.
• Logical address = (page number p, offset d). p indexes the page table (located by PTBR); entry = frame number (base address). Physical = frame:offset.
• Each process has its own page table, kept in memory → two memory accesses without a TLB.
• Offset bits = log₂(page size). VPN bits = VA bits − offset. Frame bits = PA bits − offset. Page-table size = #pages × entry size.
• Bigger pages → smaller page table, more internal fragmentation.
• Multilevel paging pages the page table. Inverted page table: one entry per frame, one table for the whole system.
theory.TLB:
• TLB = small, fast associative cache of page-table entries (page → frame).
• EMAT = H(TLB + MM) + (1 − H)(TLB + 2·MM). (If TLB time is ignored: H·MM + (1 − H)·2·MM.)
• Flushed on context switch (unless entries are wired down or tagged).
theory.Segmentation:
• User's view: variable-size segments (code, stack, functions). Address = (segment s, offset d).
• Segment table entry = (base, limit); d ≥ limit → trap; physical = base + d.
• External fragmentation. Segmentation with paging pages each segment.
theory.Virtual memory:
• Virtual memory: illusion of a memory larger than RAM using disk; swap space is on disk. Only part of a program needs to be in memory.
• Demand paging: load a page only when referenced; pure demand paging starts with zero pages.
• Page fault: referenced page not in memory → trap, find frame (victim if none), read page, update table, restart instruction. Dirty bit avoids writing back unmodified victims.
• EAT = (1 − p)·ma + p·page-fault service time; p = page-fault rate. 1 ms = 10⁶ ns. More RAM → fewer faults.
theory.Page replacement:
• FIFO: replace the oldest-loaded page; suffers Belady's anomaly (more frames can give more faults).
• Optimal: replace the page used furthest in the future; fewest faults; not implementable; benchmark.
• LRU: replace the page unused for the longest time; no Belady's anomaly (stack algorithm).
• Counting method: initial loads into empty frames are faults. Standard string 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 2 3 0 3 2 1 2 0 1 7 0 1 with 3 frames: FIFO 15, LRU 12, OPT 9.
theory.Thrashing:
• Thrashing: process spends more time paging than executing; CPU utilisation collapses as multiprogramming rises.
• Working set = pages referenced in the last Δ references. Δ too small → misses the locality; too large → overlaps several localities.
• A program has several localities that may overlap.
theory.Disk:
• Total time = seek + rotational latency + transfer. Seek = move head to the track.
• One rotation = 60 / RPM seconds; average latency = half a rotation.
• Capacity = surfaces × tracks × sectors × bytes per sector.
• Block devices (disk) transfer blocks; character devices (keyboard) bytes. Asynchronous I/O returns immediately.
theory.Disk scheduling:
• FCFS: arrival order; fair, no starvation.
• SSTF: nearest request next; lower average seek, may starve far requests.
• SCAN (elevator): go to the disk end in the current direction, then reverse.
• LOOK: like SCAN but turn at the last request.
• C-SCAN: go to the end, jump to the other end without serving, continue same direction. C-LOOK: jump from the last request to the first request at the other end.
• Total head movement = sum of |differences| along the service order (count the return jump only if the question says so).
theory.File systems:
• Allocation: contiguous (start + length; sequential & direct access; external fragmentation), linked (sequential only; pointers per block), indexed (index block; direct access).
• UNIX inode: 15 pointers = 12 direct + single, double, triple indirect.
• Free space: bit vector (1 = free) or linked list.
• Volume control block (superblock): number of blocks, block size, free-block count.
• File seek (repositioning) needs no actual I/O. Creating a file = allocate space + directory entry.
• Defragmentation makes files contiguous; compression shrinks them. NTFS supports compression.
• Access: sequential (editors/compilers), direct (databases), indexed.
theory.Kernel I/O:
• The kernel I/O subsystem keeps state tables (open-file table, device status).
• Windows NT uses message-passing I/O (I/O request packets).
theory.Protection:
• Domain = set of (object, rights-set) pairs.
• Access matrix: rows = domains/subjects, columns = objects.
• Global table = triples (domain, object, rights-set). ACL = per-object column. Capability list = per-domain row. Lock–key mechanism.
theory.Linux & shell commands:
• Navigation: pwd, cd, ls (-a hidden, -l long), mkdir (-p), rmdir (empty), rm (-r recursive, -f force), cp, mv (move/rename), touch, cat (create/concatenate/display), more/less, head/tail (10 lines).
• Search and text: grep (pattern in files), find (files), wc (-l -w -c), sort, uniq, cut.
• Permissions: r=4, w=2, x=1; chmod 755 = rwxr-xr-x, 644 = rw-r--r--; chown (owner), chgrp; umask 022 → files 644, dirs 755.
• Processes: ps, top, kill (-9), jobs, bg, fg, nice. Disk: df (free), du (usage); free (RAM).
• Redirection: > overwrite, >> append, < input, 2> errors, | pipe. $? exit status, $$ PID, $# arg count, $0 script name.
• Files: /etc (config, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow), /bin, /sbin, /home, /root, /tmp, /dev, /var/log. root UID = 0.
• vi: i/a insert, Esc command mode, :w save, :q quit, :wq, dd delete line, x delete char, r replace one char, yy copy, p paste.
• Links: ln (hard), ln -s (soft). Shells: sh, bash, csh, ksh, zsh.
• DOS: dir, copy, del, md, cd, cls, ren, type.
